lesson.title: An Alliance Against Aggression: The Founding of NATO
lesson.summary: Shaken by the Berlin Blockade, the United States broke with its long tradition of avoiding permanent peacetime alliances and joined eleven other nations in 1949 to form NATO, pledging that an attack on any member would be treated as an attack on all.
lesson.body:
The Berlin Blockade convinced American and Western European leaders that promises and economic aid alone would not deter Soviet pressure; they needed a formal military commitment. On April 4, 1949, representatives of twelve nations, the United States, Canada, Britain, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Portugal, Italy, Norway, Denmark, and Iceland, gathered in Washington DC to sign the North Atlantic Treaty, creating the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, or NATO.

The heart of the treaty was Article 5, which declared that an armed attack against one member nation would be considered an attack against them all, obligating every member to respond. This was a dramatic step for the United States. George Washington's Farewell Address in 1796 had advised the young nation to steer clear of permanent alliances, and Thomas Jefferson's first inaugural address in 1801 had echoed that caution against entangling alliances; for most of American history, foreign policy had generally avoided permanent peacetime military commitments outside the Western Hemisphere. NATO broke that tradition decisively, reflecting how thoroughly the early Cold War, and especially the shock of the Berlin Blockade, had transformed American thinking about the country's role in the world, building on the internationalist commitment the United States had already made by joining the United Nations in 1945.

NATO's purpose was straightforward: deterrence. By combining the military strength of North America and Western Europe under one collective defense guarantee, the alliance aimed to make any Soviet attack on Western Europe unthinkably costly. The Soviet Union responded to West Germany's later admission into NATO by forming its own rival alliance, the Warsaw Pact, in 1955, cementing the division of Europe into two heavily armed, opposing camps that faced off, without ever directly fighting each other, for the rest of the Cold War.
